passage:
Monday: Sumit sat down in the college library at two with his economics notes. At 2:40 Urmila appeared at the end of the row, grinning. "Chai and samosa at the gate?" Sumit went. He came back at five, notes untouched, and felt sick about the mid-sem.
Tuesday night: In his hostel room he wrote on the first page of his notebook: If someone asks me out between two and six, I'll say "Six o'clock, at the gate" and stay. He said it aloud twice, feeling a bit silly.
Thursday: At three, Urmila leaned over the table. "Chai?" Sumit's stomach tugged toward the door. "Six, at the gate. Save me a samosa." Urmila laughed and left. At six they met, and he had finished two chapters.

qa.q: What did Sumit write on the first page of his notebook?
qa.a: If someone asks me out between two and six, I'll say 'Six o'clock, at the gate' and stay.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when Urmila leaned over on Thursday, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt tempted and a little torn, since his stomach tugged toward the door, but having the words ready let him stay without a long argument with himself.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Tuesday night's plan, which named the exact obstacle and the exact reply; on Thursday Sumit didn't have to decide anything, only use the line.

qa.q: How might Urmila experience Sumit's 'Six, at the gate'?
qa.a: Urmila isn't turned away, just given a time; the laugh and the meeting at six suggest the friendship stays easy while Sumit's study hours are protected.

grounding: A student who keeps getting pulled out of the library plans a reply for a friend's invitation and goes later, so the study plan holds.

passage: Afreen, you say the college library will be too noisy with friends around? Listen to an old man. When I was nineteen, studying commerce in Pune, I lost half my afternoons to one friend, Behram. He'd lean in the doorway of the reading room: "Irani café?" And off I went. Before my second-year exams, my professor told me, "Zubin, decide now what you'll say when Behram comes, not when he's standing there." So I did. If Behram came before six, I'd say, "Six o'clock, keep a bun-maska for me," and go back to my book. The first time, my face burned. But the plan held. We still went at six, nearly every evening, and I passed with a first class.

qa.q: What did Behram ask from the doorway of the reading room?
qa.a: Behram asked, 'Irani café?'

qa.q: Why did Zubin's face burn the first time he used his line?
qa.a: He likely felt awkward and worried about seeming rude to a close friend, since refusing was new to him, even though he wanted to keep studying.

qa.q: What choice did Zubin make before his second-year exams, and why did it help?
qa.a: He decided in advance exactly what to say if Behram came before six; with the answer ready, he didn't have to win an argument with himself in the doorway.

qa.q: What might Afreen take from Zubin's story before starting college?
qa.a: Afreen might see that friends don't have to be avoided; a reply planned for the moment they turn up can protect both study time and the friendship.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a student, he planned what to say when a friend invited him out during study hours and went later instead.

passage: I'm Sarita, and last New Year's Eve I told my flatmate Himani, very grandly, "This year I'm getting healthy." I never said what that meant. I think I pictured a new version of me who simply woke up wanting salad. For about two weeks I felt it. I walked a bit, skipped some biscuits, drank more water when I remembered. Then a big audit came at work. I stayed late, ate whatever the canteen had, and walking became something I'd do "when things settle". By February I was back to my old evenings exactly, and I hadn't even noticed the day it slipped. In March Himani asked how the healthy year was going. I laughed, but it stung. There had never been a when or a how, only a mood.

qa.q: What did Sarita tell Himani on New Year's Eve?
qa.a: Sarita said, 'This year I'm getting healthy.'

qa.q: Why did the resolution feel like it was working for Sarita in the first two weeks?
qa.a: The New Year mood carried it; Sarita felt motivated and still remembered the goal, so a concrete plan didn't seem necessary.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Sarita try instead?
qa.a: Nothing tied the goal to a time or cue, so the audit pushed it aside; Sarita could pick one action linked to a moment, like a walk straight after getting home on set days.

qa.q: What might Himani have noticed before asking in March?
qa.a: Himani had probably seen the old evenings return and asked as a gentle check-in, perhaps not realising the laugh covered a sting.

grounding: An adult makes a vague resolution to get healthy with no timing or method and slides back to old habits by February.

passage:
Instructor's note, Saturday yoga, Malleswaram community hall. Rashmi, 20 February.
Jeevan signed up on 2 January, full of energy. When I asked what he wanted, he said, "To be healthier, generally. Better food, more movement, all of it." I asked which days he'd come. "Whenever I can. I'll just feel it." He came three Saturdays running. Then his sister's wedding preparations started, then a work trip, and I haven't seen him since the last week of January. Today I met him at the vegetable stall. He said, a bit sheepishly, that he was "back to the old routine" and didn't know when it happened. Next time someone joins, I'll ask for one fixed class and what comes right before it. "Whenever" seems to depend on how the week feels.

qa.q: How many Saturdays did Jeevan come before he stopped?
qa.a: He came three Saturdays running.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's sheepishness at the vegetable stall suggest?
qa.a: He seems embarrassed; he still cares about the goal and hadn't noticed it slipping away, so meeting Rashmi brought it back to mind.

qa.q: What will Rashmi ask future joiners, and why might it help?
qa.a: One fixed class and what comes right before it; a set time and cue do the remembering, so the plan doesn't depend on how the week feels.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Jeevan's drop-off?
qa.a: Rashmi doesn't treat it as laziness; the note suggests 'whenever' left Jeevan nothing to hold on to once the wedding and the work trip arrived.

grounding: A yoga instructor notes an adult whose general wish to be healthier, with no set time, faded by February.

subtype: Attaching a new action to an existing cue [Response]
passage: Amara worked at a bakery in Berlin, on her feet from five in the morning, and her back had begun to complain. Her flatmate Zeynep, a physiotherapy student, showed her four easy stretches. "Every day," Zeynep said. For two weeks Amara meant to, and mostly forgot. Evenings were for sleep; mornings were too rushed. Then one night, toothbrush in hand, she had an idea. She put her yoga mat right outside the bathroom door. Toothbrush back in the cup, straight onto the mat, four stretches, bed. No deciding. By the end of the month she'd missed only twice, both on nights she stayed at her sister's. "It's not willpower," she told Zeynep. "The toothbrush just reminds me."

qa.q: Where did Amara put her yoga mat?
qa.a: Right outside the bathroom door.

qa.q: Why did Amara keep forgetting the stretches for the first two weeks?
qa.a: Amara genuinely meant to, but she was tired in the evenings and rushed in the mornings; with no set moment, the choice quietly slipped each day.

qa.q: Which choice made the habit stick, and why?
qa.a: Linking the stretches to putting the toothbrush back in the cup; brushing already happened every night, so the stretches started without a debate.

qa.q: How might Zeynep feel seeing Amara on the mat each night?
qa.a: Zeynep might be pleased and a little surprised the stretches finally happen, and see that Amara solved a remembering problem rather than a lack of caring.

grounding: An adult attaches new stretches to brushing her teeth so they start without deliberation.

subtype: Attaching a new action to an existing cue [Response]
passage: At the working women's hostel in Chennai, the common washbasins filled up at seven, six residents brushing their teeth in a row. Lavanya, a bank clerk with a stiff neck from the counter, had tried stretching "whenever", and it happened maybe once a week. So she made a plan with her roommate, Sarika. The moment she rinsed her brush, she'd walk to the corridor window and do her neck and shoulder stretches before going back to the room. The first few mornings, the Hindi teacher from Room 12 stared. By the second week two others had joined at the window, toothpaste still on their lips. "I don't even think about it now," Lavanya told Sarika. "Brush, rinse, window."

qa.q: Where did Lavanya go right after rinsing her brush?
qa.a: She'd walk to the corridor window.

qa.q: Why had stretching 'whenever' not worked for Lavanya?
qa.a: Lavanya stayed stiff and uncomfortable because 'whenever' left stretching to her memory and mood each day, so it happened only about once a week.

qa.q: What choice did Lavanya make with Sarika, and why did it work?
qa.a: She tied the stretches to rinsing her brush, which happens every morning, so starting needed no thought: 'Brush, rinse, window.'

qa.q: What is it like for the residents who join at the window?
qa.a: Seeing Lavanya there every morning makes it feel normal and easy to copy, so they join in half-laughing, toothpaste still on their lips 🙂

grounding: An adult hooks neck stretches to rinsing her toothbrush in a hostel so she starts them without deliberating.

passage:
Sunday: Kiran, fifteen, sat down to do homework and got up four times: water, snack, messages, water again. Nothing got done. Kiran's older sister Salma said, "Try what I did in college. Pick music you love and play it only when you study."
Tuesday: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist and kept it away from every other part of the day. At five, headphones on, the first song started and Kiran was already opening the geography workbook. Maps, labels, colouring, done in forty minutes.
Friday: Maths test revision. Kiran put the playlist on but kept reading the same word problem three times, humming along. Finally the headphones came off. "This one needs quiet," Kiran told Salma. "Music's for maps."

qa.q: Which playlist did Kiran choose?
qa.a: Kiran chose the old qawwali playlist.

qa.q: What does Kiran's quick start on Tuesday suggest about how the playlist felt?
qa.a: The playlist felt like a treat Kiran had been missing, so sitting down to homework felt less like a chore and more like getting the music back.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make on Friday, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Taking the headphones off for maths; the word problems needed full attention, so Kiran saved the music for easier tasks like maps.

qa.q: How might Salma feel hearing 'Music's for maps'?
qa.a: Salma may be pleased the tip worked and that Kiran adapted it instead of copying it blindly, noticing which tasks need silence 😊

grounding: A teenager saves a favourite playlist for homework, which makes starting easier, but finds that maths needs silence.

passage: Tanvir, I see those earphones go in every time the chemistry book comes out. Let me tell you about me at fourteen, in Lucknow, long before phones. I'm your Sudha Nani, and back then our house had one radio. On Wednesday evenings it played old film songs for an hour, and I adored them. My mother made a deal: the radio was mine on Wednesdays only if my homework sat open in front of me. Suddenly I raced to the table at seven. Essays, map work, copying notes, all done humming. But algebra, never. When I tried algebra with the songs, I'd look up at the end and find the page still blank. So algebra got the quiet corner on Thursday mornings. Music helps you start. Not every task wants company.

qa.q: When did the radio play old film songs?
qa.a: On Wednesday evenings, for an hour.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha suddenly race to the table at seven?
qa.a: She adored the songs and could only have the radio with her homework open, so sitting down felt like a reward instead of a chore.

qa.q: What did Sudha do when algebra didn't work with the songs, and how could Tanvir use that?
qa.a: She moved algebra to a quiet corner on Thursday mornings; Tanvir could keep the earphones for easier work and give hard chemistry problems silence.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see those earphones differently after the story?
qa.a: Tanvir might see them as a treat worth saving for homework, while asking honestly whether the chemistry needs the music or just quiet.

grounding: A grandmother recalls reserving a favourite radio hour for homework as a teenager, which helped her start, while algebra still needed silence.

subtype: Pairing a treat with a chore [Response]
passage: In Osaka, Hiroshi, a second-year design student, had a laundry basket that never seemed to empty and a running habit that had quietly died. What he did have was a history podcast about shipwrecks that he played on every train ride. His classmate Noa, from Tel Aviv, suggested a rule: shipwrecks only while running or folding clothes. Hiroshi groaned but agreed. The first Saturday, he reached the part where the captain spots the reef just as he got back to the park gate. Rules were rules. He ran another loop to hear what happened. By the end of the month the basket was empty on Sundays and he'd run eleven times. "I'm not disciplined," he told Noa. "I just really need to know who survives."

qa.q: How many times had Hiroshi run by the end of the month?
qa.a: He'd run eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi run another loop that first Saturday?
qa.a: He badly wanted to hear what happened at the reef, and the story was only allowed while running, so his curiosity carried him past the gate 😅

qa.q: Which choice added pull to Hiroshi's dull tasks?
qa.a: Agreeing to keep the shipwreck podcast only for running and folding clothes; the story he craved became a reason to start chores he usually avoided.

qa.q: How might Noa see Hiroshi's joke about needing to know who survives?
qa.a: Noa might be amused and pleased the rule worked, seeing that the reserved story, not some new discipline, is what got Hiroshi moving.

grounding: A student allows a favourite podcast only while running or doing laundry, which pulls him into both chores.

subtype: Pairing a treat with a chore [Response]
passage: The hostel laundry room smelled of soap powder and damp concrete, and its two machines were always free, because nobody wanted to be there. Mridul used to let his clothes pile up for three weeks. This term he'd made a rule with his wingmate Sumit: the cricket-commentary podcast they both loved could be played only in the laundry room or at the college gym. Nowhere else, not even at meals. On Wednesday Sumit found Mridul sitting on an upturned bucket beside the spinning machine, one earbud in, grinning. "Last-ball finish," Mridul said. "Don't talk." His shelf was stacked with clean shirts, and his gym card had nine stamps. "Is it the gym or the podcast?" Sumit asked. Mridul shrugged. "Does it matter? I go."

qa.q: Where did Sumit find Mridul on Wednesday?
qa.a: Sitting on an upturned bucket beside the spinning machine.

qa.q: What does Mridul's grin and 'Don't talk' suggest?
qa.a: He is absorbed and happy; the podcast has turned a room nobody wanted to be in into a place he looks forward to.

qa.q: Which part of the rule makes it work, and what would weaken it?
qa.a: Keeping the podcast for the laundry room and gym only; if Mridul started playing it at meals, the treat would lose its pull toward the chores.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel about the rule after seeing Mridul on the bucket?
qa.a: Sumit may find the sight funny but also encouraging, since they share the podcast and the same rule could pull Sumit to the gym as well.

grounding: A student keeps a favourite podcast for the laundry room and gym only, which adds pull to both dull tasks.

passage: Anirban lived alone in a rented flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata, and in March he made a clever plan: the new spy series would play only on his phone, only on the gym treadmill. For two weeks it worked beautifully. Then came a Tuesday of pouring rain. "Just one episode on the sofa," he told himself. "I'll run double tomorrow." He watched three. On Thursday he was tired, so he watched on the metro home. By Sunday he'd finished the season, and his gym card showed one visit in ten days. His friend Rupam messaged: "Gym tomorrow?" Anirban stared at the finished season. There was nothing left to run toward. "Maybe next week," he typed, and felt oddly flat.

qa.q: How many visits did Anirban's gym card show in ten days?
qa.a: His gym card showed one visit in ten days.

qa.q: Why did 'Just one episode on the sofa' feel reasonable to Anirban that Tuesday?
qa.a: Rain and tiredness made the gym feel hard, and promising to run double tomorrow made breaking the rule feel like borrowing, not quitting.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what could Anirban do with the next series?
qa.a: The rainy Tuesday when the series left the treadmill; next time Anirban could keep episodes strictly for the gym, even on bad days, so the show still pulls him there.

qa.q: What might Rupam pick up from Anirban's reply?
qa.a: Rupam may sense from the flat 'Maybe next week' that the gym plan has faded, without knowing that the series used to be what got Anirban there.

grounding: An adult pairs a series with the gym, then lets it spill onto the sofa and the metro, finishes the season and stops going.

passage:
"Rehana Apa, you're home early. Isn't Thursday gym day?"
"It is. Was." Rehana dropped her bag and reached for the laptop. "Just one episode first."
"The baking show? You said that was only for the treadmill."
"I did. Then last week I watched one at home because my knee was sore. Then another because it was raining."
Her younger sister Zainab sat on the arm of the sofa. "How many gym days this month?"
"Two." Rehana winced. "And I'm on episode nineteen."
"So the show isn't pulling you to the gym anymore. It's replacing it."
"Don't be clever, Zainab." A pause. "Okay. You're right."
"Leave the laptop with me on gym days. You watch on your phone, at the gym."
Rehana hesitated, then slid the laptop across.

qa.q: Which episode was Rehana on?
qa.a: Rehana was on episode nineteen.

qa.q: Why does Rehana wince when she says 'Two'?
qa.a: She is embarrassed; the show was meant to get her to the gym, and admitting only two visits shows how far the plan has slipped.

qa.q: What choice at the end could make the bundle work again?
qa.a: Leaving the laptop with Zainab on gym days and watching only at the gym, so the show is reserved for the treadmill again.

qa.q: How does Zainab see what has happened to the plan?
qa.a: Zainab sees clearly that the show has turned from a reward into a replacement, and cares enough to say so and offer practical help, even at the risk of sounding clever.

grounding: An adult who paired a show with the gym now watches it at home instead, and her sister helps her reserve it again.

passage: The Class 10 science project was due in three weeks, and Kunal hadn't opened the kit. Every evening in their Bhopal flat he tidied his desk, sharpened pencils and watched videos of other students' models, each one better than anything he could picture making. His friend Samir had already built a solar oven. "You topped the mock," Samir said on the school bus. "Yours will be amazing." Kunal felt his throat tighten. If it wasn't amazing, everyone would know the topper was a fake. So he waited. Two nights before the deadline he finally started, with glue that wouldn't set and the stationery shop already closed. The model leaned sideways. "I didn't have time," he told the teacher, which was almost true.

qa.q: What had Samir already built?
qa.a: Samir had already built a solar oven.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's throat tighten when Samir said his model would be amazing?
qa.a: He feared an ordinary model would expose him as a 'fake' topper 😰, so not starting felt safer than finding out.

qa.q: What small step could Kunal have taken in the first week?
qa.a: Build one rough piece, like the base, with nobody watching and permission to be imperfect; starting early would have left time to fix it.

qa.q: How might Samir's praise look different if Samir knew what Kunal was feeling?
qa.a: Samir meant it kindly but might see it added pressure, and could offer to build side by side instead of predicting something amazing.

grounding: A teenager puts off a science project because a weak result would threaten his image as a topper, and the late work turns out worse.

passage:
"Simran, the debate video is due Monday. Have you recorded anything?"
"Not yet, Rekha Didi. I'm still researching."
"You've been researching for two weeks."
"It has to be good. Mrs Thomas said I have the best voice in class."
"So record a practice one. Just for me."
"No!" Simran pulled her knees up on the bed. "If it comes out bad, then she was wrong about me."
Rekha sat down beside her. "And if you record it Sunday night at eleven, what then?"
"Then it's bad because I rushed. That's different."
"Is it? Either way it's rushed, and you lose sleep too."
Simran picked at the bedsheet. "It's easier to blame the clock."
"I know. Record one line now. Just one. I'll make chai."

qa.q: Who said Simran has the best voice in class?
qa.a: Mrs Thomas said she has the best voice in class.

qa.q: What does 'It's easier to blame the clock' reveal about Simran's thinking?
qa.a: Simran is afraid of being judged: if the video is rushed, a poor result can be blamed on time rather than on her, so waiting protects her belief that she has the best voice.

qa.q: What choice does Rekha offer, and why might it work?
qa.a: Recording just one line right now, with chai; it is small enough to feel safe and breaks the wait before Sunday night makes the work worse.

qa.q: How does Rekha seem to see Simran's 'researching'?
qa.a: Rekha sees the fear under it and, rather than scolding, points out that rushing still gives a poor result, only with less sleep.

grounding: A teenager delays recording a debate video because a weak result would disprove her teacher's praise, and her sister points out the cost.

subtype: Arousal type: thrill of the deadline [Actor]
passage:
Thursday, 2:40 a.m.
Lab report due at 9. Started at 10 p.m., obviously. Honestly I love this part. Hostel's silent, heart thumping, third cup of instant coffee, and suddenly my brain is FAST. 😅 Himani knocked at midnight, saw my face and said, "Again?" I said, "This is how I work best."
Just reread the discussion section though. It's... thin. I skipped the error analysis because there was no time to redo the graph, and I copied the wrong trial numbers into Table 2 and only caught it now.
Also my eye is twitching and I have a quiz at 11.
Did I really work best, or did I just work fast? Not sure I want to know yet.
- Sarita

qa.q: When did Sarita start the lab report?
qa.a: Sarita started at 10 p.m.

qa.q: Why does the last-night rush feel good to Sarita?
qa.a: The silence, the thumping heart and the coffee make Sarita's brain feel fast, and that burst of energy feels like proof of working best under pressure.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Sarita try next time?
qa.a: The rush left no time for the error analysis and hid a copying mistake; Sarita could draft the graph and tables a few days early and keep the late burst for polishing.

qa.q: What might Himani have been thinking when asking 'Again?' at midnight?
qa.a: Himani seems worried and a little weary of the pattern, perhaps suspecting the all-nighters cost Sarita more than Sarita admits.

grounding: A student who enjoys the rush of the last night finds the energy real but the report thin and the body strained.

passage: Bhavna had finished her B.Sc. in May and had three forms open on her laptop: a lab assistant job in Nashik, a master's in Pune, and a fellowship that would place her in a village school for two years. All three closed on Friday. On Wednesday the power went out for most of the afternoon, and her phone data was nearly gone. Her brother Kunal found her sitting in the dark with the laptop at nine percent. "Just pick one and send it." "What if it's the wrong one? The fellowship is two whole years. The master's means a loan. The job might be a dead end." The battery died. Bhavna felt, strangely, relieved. On Saturday morning she opened the portal: all three closed. She hadn't said no to anything. She just hadn't said yes.

qa.q: When did all three forms close?
qa.a: All three closed on Friday.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna feel relieved when the battery died?
qa.a: Every option felt risky and hard to undo, so the dead battery took the choice out of her hands for a while and put off the fear of choosing wrong.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what small step could have helped on Wednesday?
qa.a: Waiting let the deadline choose for her; she could have sent even one or all of the forms, since applying keeps doors open and isn't the final decision.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel on Saturday seeing all three closed?
qa.a: Kunal might feel frustrated and sad for his sister after urging her to pick one, and worried about how she is taking the lost chances 😔

grounding: A graduate delays applying because each option feels risky and permanent, and the deadlines pass, making the choice by default.

passage: In the Chennai flat, Tarun's desk had two printouts taped above it: an offer letter from a logistics firm in Coimbatore and an admission letter for an MBA in Bangalore. The firm wanted an answer within two weeks. Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights. Every evening his roommate Anand asked, "Decided?" and every evening Tarun said, "Almost. I just need to be sure." What if the job was a trap? What if the loan swallowed him? On day fourteen he was still adding rows. On day fifteen the HR email arrived: the offer had gone to another candidate. Tarun stared at the screen. The MBA was the only door left, and he hadn't chosen it at all.

qa.q: What did Tarun make to compare the two options?
qa.a: Tarun made a spreadsheet of pros and cons, then a second one with weights.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep saying 'Almost. I just need to be sure'?
qa.a: Both paths looked risky and permanent to him, so staying undecided felt safer than making a wrong choice he couldn't undo.

qa.q: What turning point shows the cost of waiting, and what could Tarun have done differently?
qa.a: The HR email on day fifteen, when the job went to someone else and the choice was made for him; he could have set an earlier decision day and accepted that neither option would feel certain.

qa.q: How might Anand see those evenings of 'Decided?'
qa.a: Anand may have grown uneasy watching the spreadsheets grow while the deadline shrank, and might wish they had offered to talk it through sooner.

grounding: A graduate keeps weighing two paths because each feels risky and irreversible, until one closes and the other is left by default.

passage: Twenty minutes and two cups of tea, that's what did it. I'm Manjula, and you asked on the student radio show what I did for my friend in second year. My classmate Shreya had a design portfolio due, and every night in the hostel mess she'd say, "Tomorrow I'm starting. Properly." The next evening, nothing, and she'd look a little smaller. By the third week she'd stopped coming to our Friday movie nights. I didn't lecture her. I just knocked on her door one Sunday with the tea and said, "Twenty minutes. Together. Only the easiest bit." She chose labelling her old sketches. Twenty minutes became an hour. She didn't finish that day, but she started. Now we have a Sunday tea rule.

qa.q: What did Shreya choose as the easiest bit?
qa.a: She chose labelling her old sketches.

qa.q: Why did Shreya seem to look a little smaller each evening?
qa.a: Each broken 'tomorrow' seemed to leave her more ashamed and doubtful of herself, so the promise meant to comfort her ended up making her feel worse.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it help?
qa.a: Manjula's knock with tea and the offer of twenty minutes on the easiest bit; small and shared, it made starting feel possible instead of overwhelming.

qa.q: What was it like for Shreya to find Manjula at the door instead of a lecture?
qa.a: Probably a relief; Shreya was met with company and tea rather than judgement, which made saying yes much easier.

grounding: A friend sees a classmate keep promising to start tomorrow and feel worse, and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest part.

passage: I'm Zainab, and I share a bench with Rehana in our B.Com lectures. For a month I watched the same loop. Every Monday she'd say, "This week I start the tax assignment." Every Friday she'd say, "Monday, for sure." And each Friday she went quieter, rubbing her eyes, scrolling without really reading. I can't know exactly what was in her head, but it looked like each "tomorrow" was costing her something. Last Friday I said, "Stay after class. Twenty minutes, just you and me, and we only do the first question, the easy one." She hesitated, then nodded. We did the first question in twelve minutes. She laughed, surprised, and did the second too. On Monday she came in with three done.

qa.q: Which assignment did Rehana keep putting off?
qa.a: The tax assignment.

qa.q: What might Rehana have been feeling each Friday, and what suggests it?
qa.a: She seems increasingly discouraged: she goes quieter, rubs her eyes and scrolls without reading, as if each missed start weighed on her.

qa.q: What choice did Zainab make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Zainab offered twenty minutes after class on only the easy first question; a small, shared start broke the loop, and that success led Rehana to keep going.

qa.q: What might those twelve minutes have been like for Rehana?
qa.a: Probably a surprise and a relief 🙂; a task that had loomed for a month turned out to be doable, which made the next question feel possible.

grounding: A classmate watches a friend repeatedly promise to start and grow discouraged, and offers twenty minutes together on the easiest question.
